warmup.q: A Spark job is writing 200 Parquet files into a Hive-style table folder, dt=2026-11-07/. Halfway through, a dashboard query reads that day. What does it see?
options: Nothing from today, because Spark locks the folder while it writes
Whatever files have landed so far: part of the job's rows
All 200 files, because the reader waits for the writer
An error, because the folder is being written
warmup.why: In a folder-as-table, the table is whatever files the folder lists right now, and files land as tasks finish. There's no lock and no wait, so a reader can see part of a write. That's the gap a table format closes: in Iceberg, readers see only files a committed snapshot lists, and a commit becomes visible in one atomic step.

sections.h: A table format keeps the file list in metadata, not in the folder
sections.html:
Lesson 10's cloud warehouses never had this problem. Each keeps the list of a table's files in its own metadata service, Snowflake's cloud services layer for example, and changes that list in a transaction. The lake of lesson 4 had no such service: a Hive table was a folder. This lesson builds the open version of that metadata service out of plain files on storage, which is what a table format is.

Lesson 4 (Hive: SQL on files, partitions and the metastore) ended with three cracks in the folder-as-table model. A write is not atomic: a job's files appear one by one, and a reader in the middle sees part of the job. Listing is slow: on S3 a listing returns at most 1,000 names per request, so a partition of 50,000 files takes 50 requests before the first byte of data. And the schema is matched by name or position, so renaming a column means rewriting files or confusing readers. All three come from one decision: the folder's contents are the table.

Version 1: keep a list. Next to the data, write a file that names every data file of the table. Readers read the list instead of listing folders, which fixes the listing cost. But a writer still has to change the list, and a reader can catch the list file half rewritten.

Version 2: never change a file; write a new one. A write first puts its new data files down, which nobody reads because no list names them. Then it writes a complete new list, which also nobody reads yet. Then it switches readers from the old list to the new one in a single step. Before the switch, every reader sees the old table; after it, the new one. Nobody can see half.

That single step needs one small, mutable thing: a pointer that says which list is current, and an operation that changes it atomically: a compare-and-swap, which sets the pointer to a new value only if it still holds the value you read. Everything else is immutable files. That's the design of a table format: Apache Iceberg, Delta Lake and Apache Hudi all work this way. This lesson uses Iceberg, the one Spark, Trino, Flink, DuckDB and most other engines read and write.

The Try it shows the difference with a reader thread that counts rows while a writer adds 8 files. Copied into a plain Parquet folder one at a time, the way tasks publish their output as they finish, the reader saw 3,000, 5,000, 6,000 and 7,000 rows on the way to 8,000: tables that never existed. Appended to an Iceberg table in three commits of 8 files, the reader saw 0, 8,000, 16,000 and 24,000: whole commits and nothing in between.

Iceberg itself is a specification plus libraries, not a server or an engine. The table is files in your storage, and "the catalog" that holds the pointer can be as simple as a folder, which is what this lesson uses: a Hadoop catalog, where the warehouse is a directory tree on your disk. The demos and the lab use Iceberg 1.12.0 (September 2026) with Spark 4.1.4, the newest Spark line 1.12 has a runtime for (lesson 9).

try.title: Count rows while a writer adds files
steps: Run AtomicCommitDemo. A reader thread counts rows in a loop while the main thread adds files: first to a plain Parquet folder, one file a second, then to an Iceberg table, in three commits.
Predict the set of counts the reader will see in each case.
In the plain-folder case, each file appears whole (it's renamed into place). Why does the reader still see a partial write?

code.title: AtomicCommitDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.batch.l11.demo import java.io.File import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentSkipListSet import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicBoolean import kotlin.concurrent.thread /** * A reader counts rows in a loop while a writer adds 8 files. First into a plain Parquet folder, * one file a second, the way a job's tasks publish their files as they finish. Then into an * Iceberg table, as one commit. Prints every count the reader saw. */ fun main() { val spark = demoSpark() val staged = File("build/l09/staged").apply { deleteRecursively() } payments(spark, 0, 8_000, files = 8).write().parquet(staged.absolutePath) // 8 files of 1,000 rows val files = staged.listFiles { f -> f.name.endsWith(".parquet") }!!.sorted() fun watch(count: () -> Long, write: () -> Unit): Set<Long> { val seen = ConcurrentSkipListSet<Long>() val done = AtomicBoolean(false) val reader = thread { while (!done.get()) runCatching { seen += count() } } Thread.sleep(500) write() Thread.sleep(500) done.set(true) reader.join() return seen } // a folder table: the file listing IS the table, so every new file is visible the moment it lands val folder = File("build/l09/plain").apply { deleteRecursively(); mkdirs() } val schema = spark.read().parquet(staged.absolutePath).schema() val plain = watch({ spark.read().schema(schema).parquet(folder.absolutePath).count() }) { for (f in files) { // copy under a hidden name, then rename: each single file appears whole val tmp = File(folder, ".${f.name}.tmp") f.copyTo(tmp) tmp.renameTo(File(folder, f.name)) Thread.sleep(1_000) // a task finishing every second } } println("plain folder, 8 files added one by one, the reader saw: $plain") // an Iceberg table: the files are written first, then one commit makes all of them visible spark.sql("CREATE TABLE lake.pay.atomic ($PAYMENT_COLUMNS) USING iceberg") val iceberg = watch({ spark.table("lake.pay.atomic").count() }) { repeat(3) { spark.read().parquet(staged.absolutePath).writeTo("lake.pay.atomic").append() } } println("Iceberg table, 3 commits of 8 files each, the reader saw: $iceberg") spark.stop() }

try.expect:
plain folder, 8 files added one by one, the reader saw: [0, 3000, 5000, 6000, 7000, 8000]
Iceberg table, 3 commits of 8 files each, the reader saw: [0, 8000, 16000, 24000]

In the plain folder every file landed whole, because it was renamed into place, and the reader still saw partial tables: for a folder-as-table, each new file is visible the moment it lands, and a job of 8 files is 8 separate moments. Which partial counts you catch depends on how fast your machine runs the reader's queries, so your list will differ; the point is that it has values between 0 and 8,000. The Iceberg reader only ever saw multiples of 8,000. Each commit wrote its 8 files first, where no snapshot pointed at them, and then made all of them visible in one swap.

sections.h: Iceberg's metadata is a tree of files that are never edited
sections.html:
Version 2 above had a single list file. Write it as one file and every commit must rewrite the whole list: a table of a million files gets a new million-line file for a commit that adds ten. Iceberg splits the list into a tree, so a commit rewrites only a small top and reuses everything below.

From the top, as the figure shows:

  1. The table metadata file, v4.metadata.json. JSON, one per version of the table. It holds the schemas (every column with a permanent field id), the partition specs, the table properties, and the list of snapshots: the table's versions. Each snapshot has an id, its parent's id, a timestamp, a summary, and the path of its manifest list. One of them is current.
  2. The manifest list, one Avro file per snapshot. (Avro is a compact binary format that stores records one after another, with the schema in the file's header.) One row per manifest, with the range of partition values inside it, so a query on one day can skip whole manifests without opening them.
  3. The manifests, Avro files with one row per data file: its path, its partition value, its row count, its size, and per-column statistics, including the minimum and maximum of each column. Lesson 5's footer statistics, moved up into the table's metadata, so a reader can skip a file without opening it.
  4. The data files: plain Parquet.

A commit that appends 8 files writes 8 data files, one new manifest, one new manifest list that names the new manifest plus all the old ones, and one new metadata file. The old manifests are reused as they are. That's why the snapshots are cheap: snapshot S2 and snapshot S3 share every manifest that didn't change.

A reader walks the tree from the top: pointer, metadata file, current snapshot, its manifest list, the manifests whose partition ranges can match, the data files whose statistics can match. It never lists a folder. In the Try it, a create and three appends left four metadata JSON files (one per version), three manifest lists (one per snapshot), three manifests and nine data files, three days per append. Spark also exposes the tree as metadata tables you can query: lake.pay.payments.snapshots, .manifests, .files, .history.

sections.h: A commit is one compare-and-swap of the table pointer
sections.html:
Everything in the tree is written once and never changed. The only thing a commit changes is the pointer, and that's where concurrency is handled.

A commit, step by step, as the stepper shows: write the data files; write a manifest for them; write a manifest list for the new snapshot; write the new metadata file, which lists the new snapshot as current and keeps the old ones. Up to here nobody can see anything. Then swap the pointer from the old metadata file to the new one, if and only if it still names the old one. That condition makes the swap a compare-and-swap, and it's the whole commit protocol.

What if two writers start from v7 at once? Both build their new metadata on v7. The first to swap wins and the table moves to v8. The second swap fails, because the pointer no longer says v7. The loser doesn't wait on a lock; it reloads v8, checks that its change still makes sense (for an append, it always does), re-applies it on top of v8, and swaps again. This is optimistic concurrency: no locks while working, a check at the end, and a retry when the check fails. Iceberg's docs call the result serializable isolation: all changes form one linear history. The retry is cheap because the data files and the new manifest are reused, and only the small files at the top are written again.

Where the pointer lives depends on the catalog. In the Hadoop catalog of this lesson it's the metadata files themselves: a commit writes v8.metadata.json under a temporary name and renames it into place, and the rename fails if v8 already exists; version-hint.text then tells readers where to start. That needs an atomic "create only if nobody has", which HDFS and your laptop give through rename. Lesson 3 showed that an object store is not a file system: for years S3 had no rename at all and no way to say "only if absent", so two writers could both write v8 and the last one silently won. That's why Delta Lake's documentation for S3 still asks for every writer of a table to go through one Spark driver, or through a DynamoDB table for mutual exclusion. Since 2024 S3 has conditional writes. A PUT with If-None-Match: * creates an object only if the key doesn't exist yet (August 2024), and If-Match replaces it only if its ETag is still the one you read (November 2024). Those are exactly the two forms of compare-and-swap a commit needs: "create v8 only if nobody has" and "move the pointer only if it still names v7". Production Iceberg tables still keep the pointer in a catalog with a database or service behind it (lesson 12), because the catalog also names tables, controls access and serves every engine, but the store itself can now take part in a commit safely.

The old snapshots are still in the metadata, and each one still names exactly the files it had. That gives you time travel: SELECT ... FROM t VERSION AS OF <snapshot id> or TIMESTAMP AS OF '<time>' reads the table as it was. Readers also get isolation for free: a query that started on S1 keeps reading S1's files even if S2 commits halfway through. The window ends when old snapshots are expired and their files deleted, a clean-up job lesson 12 covers.

try.title: Lose a commit race, then read the past
steps: Run CommitDemo. Two writers load the same table version. Writer A commits a property change with Iceberg's low-level commit(base, new); writer B then tries the same from its stale base. Then B retries through the normal API, and the demo appends twice more and time-travels.
Predict what B's first attempt does, and which metadata file the table ends up at.

The first commit wins the swap; the second * is refused, then retried on top of the new version. Then time travel. */ fun main() { val spark = demoSpark() spark.sql("CREATE TABLE lake.pay.ledger ($PAYMENT_COLUMNS) USING iceberg PARTITIONED BY (days(created_at))") payments(spark, 0, 1_000).writeTo("lake.pay.ledger").append() val firstCommitAt = System.currentTimeMillis() Thread.sleep(50) val location = tableDir("pay", "ledger").absolutePath val tables = HadoopTables(spark.sparkContext().hadoopConfiguration()) // two writers load the table: both see the same current version val tableA = tables.load(location) val tableB = tables.load(location) val a = (tableA as HasTableOperations).operations() val b = (tableB as HasTableOperations).operations() val baseA = a.current() val baseB = b.current() println("writer A and writer B both start from ${baseA.metadataFileLocation().substringAfterLast('/')}") // the low-level commit: "replace base with this new metadata", a compare-and-swap a.commit(baseA, TableMetadata.buildFrom(baseA).setProperties(mapOf("settlement.run" to "A")).build()) println("A commits: the table is now at ${a.current().metadataFileLocation().substringAfterLast('/')}") try { b.commit(baseB, TableMetadata.buildFrom(baseB).setProperties(mapOf("settlement.run" to "B")).build()) } catch (e: CommitFailedException) { println("B commits from the old base: CommitFailedException: ${e.message!!.substringBefore(": /")}") } // the normal API, on B's same stale table object: it reloads the current version, applies // the change to it and swaps; if the swap loses again, it repeats (commit.retry.num-retries) tableB.updateProperties().set("settlement.run", "B").commit() val now = tables.load(location) println("B retries on top of A: the table is at ${(now as HasTableOperations).operations().current().metadataFileLocation().substringAfterLast('/')}, " + "settlement.run = ${now.properties()["settlement.run"]}") // two more appends, then read the past payments(spark, 1_000, 500).writeTo("lake.pay.ledger").append() payments(spark, 1_500, 500).writeTo("lake.pay.ledger").append() val history = spark.sql("SELECT snapshot_id, parent_id, operation FROM lake.pay.ledger.snapshots ORDER BY committed_at").collectAsList() println("snapshots: " + history.joinToString { "${it.getLong(0)} (${it.getString(2)})" }) println("now: %,d rows".format(spark.table("lake.pay.ledger").count())) println("VERSION AS OF the first snapshot: %,d rows".format( spark.sql("SELECT count(*) FROM lake.pay.ledger VERSION AS OF ${history.first().getLong(0)}").first().getLong(0))) println("TIMESTAMP AS OF just after the first commit: %,d rows".format( spark.sql("SELECT count(*) FROM lake.pay.ledger TIMESTAMP AS OF CAST($firstCommitAt / 1000.0 AS TIMESTAMP)").first().getLong(0))) spark.stop() }

sections.h: Columns have ids and partitions are derived from columns
sections.html:
Two more consequences of keeping the truth in metadata: columns can change without rewriting data, and partitions become a property of the table rather than of your queries.

Start with columns. Every column gets a permanent field id when it's created, and Iceberg writes that id into the Parquet files next to the name. Readers match a file's columns to the table's by id. So renaming amount_cents to amount_minor is a metadata change: the id stays, old files still match, and no data file is touched. Adding a column gives it a new id that no old file has, so old rows read NULL. Dropping a column removes it from the schema, and its data in old files is simply never read again. Iceberg's docs list add, drop, rename, reorder and type widening, all without rewriting files. Compare a folder of Parquet matched by name: drop amount_cents, add a new amount_cents, and the old values come back from the dead.

Partitions move into the metadata too. Lesson 4's Hive table needed a dt string column, and a query that filtered on created_at instead of dt read every partition. Iceberg partitions by a transform of a real column: PARTITIONED BY (days(created_at)), or hours(...), months(...), bucket(16, merchant_id), truncate(...). There's no extra column. Writers compute the partition value, the manifests record it, and a query that filters on created_at gets the matching days worked out for it. That's hidden partitioning. In the Try it, a one-day filter on created_at plans 1 of the 3 data files.

The layout itself can change. When a table outgrows its layout, ALTER TABLE ... ADD PARTITION FIELD bucket(4, merchant_id) starts a new partition spec. New files use it, old files keep the spec they were written with, and the planner prunes each group of files with its own spec. Nothing is rewritten.

All of this is format version 2, which Iceberg 1.12 still creates by default. Format version 3 is adopted in the spec, and Iceberg 1.12 with Spark 4.1 can create and write v3 tables. It adds deletion vectors for row-level deletes, the VARIANT type from lesson 9, geometry and geography types, default column values, nanosecond timestamps, and row lineage, a stable _row_id for every row. Ask for it with TBLPROPERTIES ('format-version' = '3'), as the Try it does, after checking that every engine that reads the table supports v3 and the v3 features you need.

Iceberg partitioning: hidden partitioning and transforms

analogy: An Iceberg table works like a Git repository. The Parquet files are blobs: written once, never changed. Each metadata file is a commit: it records the whole state of the table and points back to its parent. The catalog's pointer is the branch ref, main, naming the current commit. Writing data is like git commit: you create new blobs and a new commit object, and nothing changes for anyone until the ref moves. Moving the ref is a compare-and-swap, like a push that is rejected when someone else pushed first, after which you rebase and push again. Time travel is git checkout of an old commit. The analogy breaks at the history: Git keeps every commit forever, while an Iceberg table expires old snapshots on a schedule and deletes the files only they used, so time travel only reaches as far back as the snapshots you kept.
world: The commit protocol is one you already use. An optimistic lock on your Oracle ledger (UPDATE accounts SET balance = :b, version = version + 1 WHERE id = :id AND version = :v, retry if zero rows changed) is the same compare-and-swap Iceberg does on its table pointer. The Kafka log gives you replay by offset; an Iceberg table gives you replay by snapshot, so a nightly reconciliation job can record the snapshot id it read, and an auditor can run the same query against that exact snapshot next month. And the idempotency key on your payment API has a cousin here: Iceberg 1.12 added idempotency keys to the REST catalog protocol, so a writer whose commit request times out can retry without committing the same data twice.
mistake: The common mistake is treating an Iceberg table's folder as the table: listing data/ to find the files, copying Parquet files into it to "add" data, or deleting files from it to remove a bad day. None of that changes the table, because the table is whatever the current snapshot's manifests list. A copied-in file is invisible to every reader, and a deleted file breaks every snapshot that still lists it, with a missing-file error on the next read. People do it because a Hive table was its folder (lesson 4), and old scripts still treat it that way. Go through the table instead: INSERT, DELETE, CALL system.add_files(...) to register existing files, CALL system.expire_snapshots(...) and remove_orphan_files to clean up. Let the commit protocol decide what's in the table.

drill.title: Iceberg in five statements
drill.prompt: From memory, write the Spark SQL to: create a payments table partitioned by the day of created_at with hidden partitioning; list its snapshots; read it as of a snapshot id; rename amount_cents to amount_minor; and start bucketing new data by merchant_id into 16 buckets. Then say which of the five rewrites a data file.

answer.html: CREATE TABLE lake.pay.payments (payment_id BIGINT, merchant_id INT, amount_cents BIGINT, created_at TIMESTAMP) USING iceberg PARTITIONED BY (days(created_at)); SELECT snapshot_id, parent_id, operation FROM lake.pay.payments.snapshots; SELECT * FROM lake.pay.payments VERSION AS OF 4764547682752508805; ALTER TABLE lake.pay.payments RENAME COLUMN amount_cents TO amount_minor; ALTER TABLE lake.pay.payments ADD PARTITION FIELD bucket(16, merchant_id); -- none of them rewrites a data file: the last two only write a new metadata file, -- and old files keep the partition spec they were written with

recap: A table format keeps the list of a table's files in metadata files next to the data, so readers never list folders and a write becomes visible in one step.
Iceberg's metadata is a tree of immutable files: a pointer, a metadata JSON (schemas, partition specs, snapshots), one manifest list per snapshot, manifests with per-file stats, then Parquet files.

A commit writes new files and then swaps the table pointer from the old metadata file to the new one. If someone else swapped first, the writer re-applies its change and tries again: optimistic concurrency.
Every snapshot still lists its files, so VERSION AS OF and TIMESTAMP AS OF read the past until the snapshot is expired.

Columns are tracked by id, so rename, add and drop are metadata changes. Partitions are transforms of columns (days(created_at)), so queries filter on the column and the layout can change without rewriting old files.

explain.prompt: Explain to a colleague who knows Hive tables why an Iceberg INSERT is all-or-nothing for readers, using the files the commit writes and the order it writes them in.
explain.answer: A Hive table is its folder: whatever files are in dt=2026-11-03/ right now are the table, so a reader that lists the folder halfway through a write sees half the write. An Iceberg table is whatever its current snapshot lists, and readers find files only through that list. A commit writes in a fixed order. First the new Parquet data files, which no snapshot names yet, so nobody can see them. Then a manifest listing those files with their partition values and stats, then a new manifest list naming the old manifests plus the new one, then a new metadata file that adds the snapshot and makes it current. Up to here, every reader still opens the old metadata file and sees the old table. The last step is one atomic swap of the table pointer from the old metadata file to the new one; in a Hadoop catalog that's a rename that fails if the target exists, in a REST or JDBC catalog a compare-and-swap in the catalog. A reader that starts before the swap sees the old snapshot, one that starts after sees the new one, and none can see a mix. If the job dies before the swap, the files it wrote are orphans that no snapshot lists, cleaned up later, and the table never changed.

deeper.html:
The Hadoop catalog used in this lesson is the simplest catalog, and it's for learning and for HDFS. It relies on the file system's rename failing when the target exists; Iceberg's documentation for HadoopCatalog says the file system must support atomic rename, which object stores like S3 don't offer. Production tables use a catalog that keeps the pointer in a database and does the compare-and-swap there: the Hive metastore, a JDBC catalog, AWS Glue, or a REST catalog server such as Apache Polaris. Lesson 12 covers catalogs and the REST protocol.

Old snapshots cost storage: every file any kept snapshot lists stays on disk. CALL system.expire_snapshots(...) removes old snapshots from the metadata and deletes the files only they used, and the time travel window ends there. Small appends also pile up small files and small manifests; rewrite_data_files and rewrite_manifests compact them in a new commit. Lesson 12 covers both, along with row-level deletes and updates.

Format versions: v1 described append-only analytic tables; v2 added row-level deletes with delete files; v3, now adopted, adds binary deletion vectors, the VARIANT type (the same one Spark 4 has, lesson 9), geometry and geography types, default column values, row lineage (_row_id, _last_updated_sequence_number) and nanosecond timestamps. Iceberg 1.12 still creates v2 tables unless you set 'format-version' = '3', as the EvolutionDemo does. Version 4 is in development; its draft replaces the manifest list with a root manifest in an adaptive tree, so a small commit writes fewer metadata files.
